newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks soar to record close on loan payment.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks soar to record close on loan payment.

text.p: Mexican stocks gained sharply to notch up their seventh record close in eight sessions Wednesday in the wake of news that Mexico would prepay $5 billion on international loans, traders said.
"It really heated up at the close. The rally certainly looks like continuing apace. The number of trades and volume were overwhelming," a trader said.
The leading IPC share index ended up 96.66 points, or 2.66 percent, at 3,728.02. Volume was a very heavy 190.8 million shares, and an almost-unheard-of 7,067 trades were settled.

In the opening minutes of trade, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz announced Mexico will pay the U.S. Treasury $3.5 billion outstanding on an emergency loan made in February 1995 and an additional $1.5 billion to the International Monetary Fund.
Market euphoria was such that Mexican shares and American Depository Receipts shunned a slump in the Dow Jones, which closed down 0.52 percent at 6,726.88 points, the trader added.
"The Dow didn't even make a dent," he said.
Market heavyweight Telmex ADRs rallied 1-1/8 to 39 on Wall Street, while their L series shares in Mexico gained 80 centavos (10 cents) to 15.50 pesos ($1.99).
Analysts said the rally was also fuelled by a fortuitous combination of other economic news.

"There was a bit of everything, and all of it was good; international reserves, industrial output, exchange rate stability and falling rates were all essential for the bourse today," said Leonor Gonzalez, technical analyst at the BBV-Probursa brokerage.
On Tuesday evening, Banco de Mexico had announced its net international reserves as of Jan. 10 were up to $17.863 billion, from $17.651 billion Jan 3.
Also Tuesday evening, the central bank put the bellwether 28-day Treasury bill at 22.98 percent, a fall of 1.26 percentage points from last week's primary auction.
Despite the sharp fall in primary rates, the benchmark 48-hour peso softened just 0.4 of a centavo to 7.8030/7.8080 per dollar.
In late trade, the Finance Ministry said November 1996 industrial production was up 11.8 percent in year-on-year terms.
Traders and analyst also drew attention to the performance by Telmex shares and ADRs.
"Telmex ADRs weakening resistance, and the pace set by their price, is very interesting. At this rate, we see their next resistance at $42.5," Gonzalez added.
"The way ADRs took off today was impressive. That shook up many quiet stocks," a trader at the Valburmex brokerage said.
Traders also noted the Inbursa brokerage made a cross trade of 20 million shares in the opening minutes of trade in Telmex, with which it has corporate linkss.
"When we saw such a hefty trade in Telmex, well the rest of us did the same to get on the bandwagon," one dealer said.
On the broad market, a total of 125 stocks changed hands, of which gainers outnumbered decliners by 71 to 30.

Dealers noted the presence of construction firm Tribasa near the head of the leaders' list, on the back of its ADRs, they said. Tribasa's nominal shares gained 1.94 pesos (25 cents) to 21.40 pesos ($2.74), while its ADRs ended up 50 cents at $5.50.
Dealers said the list of declining issues was headed by illiquid stocks after small, unrepresentative trades.

Amid the euphoria, analysts noted that. whereas Mexican stocks had closed at a record in peso terms, in dollar terms they were still well down compared to levels reached before the December 1994 devaluation crisis.

Using Reuters data, the dollar-adjusted IPC closed at 478.01 on Wednesday, compared to 672.33 on Dec. 16, 1994, the last trading day before a suuden devaluation of the peso sent the Mexican economy tumbling into its worst recession in five decades.
"It is so hard to forget December 1994," one analyst said.
